Pretreatment of OpvE inhibited H2O2-induced oxidative stress and protected against LPS-induced inflammatory injury by respectively regulating the Nrf2/HO-1/COX2 and TLR4/MYD88 signaling pathways. OpvE also showed anti-S. aureus properties with a MIC of 1.2 mg/mL, and with this concentration, OpvE produced an 8.3 ± 0.16 mm inhibition zone on a bacterial plate. Conclusions: This work highlighted the phytochemical character and some bioactivities, as well as the underline mechanism, which would support the further studies and application of O. vulgatum Linn.

articles.title: Contrasting Spatial Genomic Structure in Two Widespread Grassland Species Across Norway Supports Species-Specific Seed Sourcing.
articles.abstract: Ecological restoration typically relies on locally sourced seed material, yet seed sourcing in many countries is based on broad administrative regions rather than empirical genetic data. Whether these generalized zones reflect biologically meaningful population genomic structure, particularly among co-occurring species used together in restoration, remains poorly understood, thus limiting genetically informed restoration practices. Here, we use genome-wide double-digest RAD sequencing (ddRAD-seq) to examine spatial population genomic structure in two widespread perennial grassland species commonly used in restoration in Norway: Silene dioica, an obligately outcrossing species with limited seed dispersal, and Achillea millefolium, a polyploid complex characterized by high gene flow and dispersal capacity. Analysis of 17 populations of S. dioica (355 individuals; 19,200 SNPs) and 23 populations of A. millefolium (428 individuals; 21,294 SNPs) across broad latitudinal and climatic gradients in Norway revealed strikingly contrasting patterns of genetic structure. Silene dioica showed moderate spatial structure, significant isolation-by-distance, and multiple geographically coherent genetic groups, indicating spatially restricted gene flow and supporting the delineation of multiple seed transfer zones. In contrast, A. millefolium showed weak population differentiation, extensive admixture, and little geographic structuring, but significant isolation-by-environment, with annual precipitation emerging as the strongest environmental predictor of genomic differentiation independently of geographic distance, justifying the delineation of three broad genomic zones. Because species-specific life-history traits likely contributed to these patterns, a single generalized seed-sourcing framework can be inadequate even for sympatric species restored together. While the structured genomic patterns in S. dioica support localized seed sourcing, the high connectivity in A. millefolium supports broader transfer zones. Overall, our study highlights the importance of incorporating genomic data into restoration planning by aligning seed transfer distances with species-specific connectivity to reduce genetic risks and maintain evolutionary potential under environmental change.

articles.title: Metabolomic Fingerprinting and UHPLC-ESI-HRMS/MS Profiling of Five Medicinal Plants Associated with Wound Care.
articles.abstract: Chronic wounds remain a challenging medical problem due to the involvement of multiple biological processes that can delay normal tissue repair. Medicinal plants may contain diverse bioactive compounds with potential relevance for wound management. However, detailed characterization of their chemical composition is essential for understanding their biological potential. The phytochemical composition of five medicinal plants, Verbena officinalis, Plantago major, Achillea millefolium, Hypericum perforatum, and Calendula officinalis, was investigated using ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography coupled with high-resolution electrospray ionization tandem mass spectrometry (UHPLC-ESI-HRMS/MS). A total of 162 metabolites were identified across the investigated extracts, representing diverse classes including flavonoids, phenolic acids, phenylethanoid glycosides, xanthones, naphthodianthrones, acylphloroglucinols and iridoid glycosides. A comparison with the available literature data and databases confirmed previously reported constituents and revealed 115 unique compounds that had not previously been reported for at least one of the five investigated plant species. The obtained results demonstrate the remarkable chemical diversity of the selected medicinal plants and provide a comprehensive basis for further investigation of their biological activities and potential use in multicomponent herbal mixtures for wound management.

articles.title: DNA metabarcoding reveals key floral resources for native pollinators in post-fire landscapes.
articles.journal: Ecological applications : a publication of the Ecological Society of America
articles.abstract: Wildfires are a natural disturbance in dry ponderosa pine forest ecosystems, and are increasing in frequency and severity across western North America. The effects of wildfire on biotic and abiotic conditions have important implications for higher trophic levels, including native bees. We sought to quantify the responses of flowering plants to fire age and severity and determine the effects of these shifts on pollinator richness through time. We sequenced pollen from pan and blue vane traps deployed every 2 weeks from April to August in 2022 and 2023 to quantify shifts in foraging resources for pollinator communities in landscapes aged 1-8 years post-fire, and in an unburned area. DNA metabarcoding pollen suspended in blue vane and pan traps revealed herbaceous perennials such as Achillea millefolium, Lupinus spp., and Phacelia hastata to be key floral resources for post-fire pollinator communities. Burn age and burn severity were the main drivers of plant-pollinator richness, and plant species richness increased with burn age and burn severity. Bee species richness varied among burn severities, supporting management for patch mosaics and landscape heterogeneity as a fundamental principle of fire reintroduction. Our findings underscore the importance of bioinformatics threshold selection in plant list generation and highlight the role of burn age, burn severity, and plant richness in effectively conserving pollinator species across fire-effected landscapes. This study also used the novel approach of collecting pollen suspended in trap solutions to quantify floral resources for insect pollinators, highlighting the utility of trap byproducts to provide insightful ecological information. Understanding post-fire plant-pollinator relationships is critical for successful conservation of dry forest angiosperm flora and bee faunas.

articles.title: Phytochemical-Mediated Redox Synthesis of Selenium Nanoparticles Under Sunlight: Mechanistic and Bioactivity Insights.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION/OBJECTIVE: Selenium nanoparticles are recognized for their significant biomedical potential; however, conventional synthesis methods often rely on toxic reagents and energy- intensive processes. Green, plant-mediated synthesis offers a sustainable alternative, although controlling particle size and maintaining high colloidal stability remain challenging. This study aimed to establish a green, sunlight-assisted biosynthesis route for SeNPs using dual extracts of Achillea millefolium and Echinops spp., optimized through response surface methodology. METHODS: Synthesis conditions were optimized using a central composite design. The optimized SeNPs were characterized by UV-Vis spectroscopy, DLS, FT-IR, XRD, and SEM-EDX analyses. They were further evaluated for antioxidant and antibacterial activities. RESULTS: The quadratic RSM models demonstrated good predictive capability (R² = 0.97-0.99). Optimal conditions (1000 μL extract, 30 mL Na₂SeO₃ and 5 minutes of sunlight exposure) produced spherical SeNPs with a mean hydrodynamic diameter of 40.6 nm (range: 38-80 nm), a PDI of 0.36-0.55 and a strongly negative zeta potential (-31.4 mV). A characteristic absorption peak at 550 nm confirmed nanoparticle formation. The synthesized SeNPs exhibited considerable antioxidant activity (DPPH inhibition: 72% at 100 μg/mL; IC₅₀ = 71.9 μg/mL) as well as antibacterial activity against Staphylococcus aureus (MIC = 62.5 μg/mL) and Escherichia coli (MIC = 125 μg/mL). DISCUSSION: These findings demonstrate that the dual-plant, sunlight-assisted synthesis strategy provides an effective green approach to producing stable SeNPs with favorable physico-chemical characteristics and promising biological activities. CONCLUSION: This dual-extract, sunlight-assisted approach provides a rapid (5 min), environmentally benign, and cost-effective method for producing stable and biofunctional SeNPs with promising antioxidant and antibacterial properties.

articles.title: Biological and Phytochemical Profile of Volatile Oils from Romanian Mountain Flora.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Essential oils (EOs) are complex mixtures extracted from plants. The aim of this study was to evaluate the chemical composition, antioxidant and antimicrobial properties, as well as in vivo toxicity against Drosophila melanogaster of the EOs extracted from Achillea millefolium L. (AM), Mentha longifolia L. (ML), and Thymus serpyllum L. (TS) from the mountains in Sibiu County, Romania. Methods: EOs were extracted by hydrodistillation. Their phytocompounds were determined by Gas Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry. Antioxidant potential was evaluated by 2,2-diphenyl-1-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH), 2,2'-azinobis [3-ethylbenzothiazoline-6-sulfonic acid]-diammonium salt (ABTS), and ferric-reducing antioxidant power (FRAP) assays. Antibacterial action was measured against eight pathogenic bacteria. An in vivo D. melanogaster diet-dependent viability assay was conducted to assess the toxicity of the EOs. Results: Chamazulene (49.72%), pulegone (36.20%), and thymol (42.11%) were the most abundant constituents of the AM, ML, and TS EOs, respectively. All tested EOs exerted antioxidant activity, with TS EO being the most efficient in the DPPH (98.19% inhibition) and ABTS (1.82 mmol Trolox equivalent (TE)/mL EO) scavenging assays, while AM EO performed best in the FRAP assay (66.70 μmol TE/mL EO). Against TS EO, Bacillus subtilis was the most sensitive, with an inhibition zone of 37 mm. A dose-dependent decrease in the viability of D. melanogaster L. was observed when their diet was supplemented with AM, ML, and TS EOs. Conclusions: The analyzed EOs demonstrated antioxidant and antimicrobial effects, suggesting their potential applications in various fields. However, due to their toxicity, an in-depth analysis is required before introducing such products in therapy.

articles.title: Comparative efficacy of topical garlic extract and 20% podophyllin solution in the treatment of female genital warts: a triple-blind randomized clinical trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Genital warts caused by human papillomavirus are common sexually transmitted infections, with no single therapy providing consistent clearance. Garlic extract has antiviral and antiproliferative properties and may offer a low-cost treatment. OBJECTIVE: To compare the efficacy and safety of topical 5% garlic extract with 20% podophyllin solution in women with genital warts. METHODS: Seventy-four women were randomized to 5% garlic extract (n = 37) or 20% podophyllin (n = 37), applied weekly for four weeks. Wart size and count were assessed using marginal models (generalized estimating equations). The primary outcome was change in mean wart size and the secondary outcome was change in wart count. RESULTS: Mean wart size decreased from 1.61 ± 0.81 to 0.60 ± 0.82 mm with garlic extract and from 2.96 ± 7.99 to 0.62 ± 0.73 mm with podophyllin. The between-group p-value at final assessment was 0.756; group × time interaction p values were 0.329 for wart size and 0.583 for count. Among 35 and 37 participants analyzed, complete response occurred in 18 (51.4%) and 19 (51.4%), respectively; complete or partial response occurred in 23 (65.7%) and 25 (67.6%). Itching and burning occurred in 8 (21.6%) garlic-treated participants each. CONCLUSION: Both treatments reduced wart size and count, with similar response rates. Four-week follow-up precluded assessment of durability and recurrence.

articles.title: Harnessing nature: a systematic exploration of in vitro antileishmanial and antihuman African trypanosomal properties in traditional medicinal plants and their active principles.
articles.abstract: CONTEXT: Current treatments for leishmaniasis and Human African Trypanosomiasis (HAT) are constrained by toxicity, high costs, and the growing threat of parasite resistance. In this context, natural products have emerged as promising alternatives, offering the potential for safer and more cost‑effective therapeutic interventions. OBJECTIVE: This review assesses the antileishmanial and antitrypanosomal activities of medicinal plants, underscoring their significance in addressing parasitic diseases and identifying promising candidates for future drug discovery and development. METHODS: Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted for literature published between 2003 and 2023. Studies were considered eligible if they reported in vitro activities of extracts or compounds against Leishmania spp. or Trypanosoma brucei with IC50 < 10 µg/mL. Data included plant species, extraction methods, parasite strains, active compound(s), cytotoxicity profiles, and traditional uses. The quality of each study was evaluated based on the reproducibility of experimental procedures. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS: A total of fifty eligible articles were included. 217 plants demonstrated potent activity (IC₅。 < 10 µg/mL) against Leishmania spp. and/or T. brucei. Among these, 41 species had documented traditional use in the treatment of leishmaniasis or HAT, whereas 76 were traditionally employed for unrelated ailments yet exhibited scientific evidence of antiparasitic efficacy. Notably, 67 species were active against both parasites, 120 displayed selective antitrypanosomal, and 30 showed selective antileishmanial activities. Exemplary candidates include Achillea ptarmica L. (pellitorine), Allium sativum L. (allicin, ajoene), Strychnos spinosa Lam. (triterpenoids), Tridax procumbens L. (oxylipin), and Marrubium incanum Desr. (salvigenin). More studies should define mechanisms and in vivo efficacy.Systematic review registration: Not registered.

articles.title: Evaluation of phyto-additive mixture on growth performances and immunoprotection against white feces syndrome in Pacific white shrimp, Penaeus vannamei.
articles.abstract: Disease outbreaks like white feces syndrome significantly effecting shrimp farming productivity, and one of the primary challenges is enhancing the innate immune system of shrimp to improve resilience against Vibrio-associated diseases. Phyto-additives provide an eco-friendly approach to sustainable shrimp farming by improving growth, antioxidant defences, modulating immune responses, and strengthening resistance to pathogenic infections, while reducing dependence on synthetic compounds. To address these challenges, this study evaluated a dietary phyto-additive mixture containing crude extracts of Syzygium cumini, Withania somnifera, Curcuma longa, Allium sativum, Argemone mexicana and lemon peel on the growth performance, digestibility, and immune response of Penaeus vannamei against white feces syndrome. 540 juvenile shrimp (1.14 ± 0.05 g) were randomly distributed into six treatment groups in triplicate (30 shrimp/tank). Six experimental diets were formulated by supplementing the basal diet with 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4, and 0.5 g 100 g-1 of the phyto-additive mixture, designated as Control, T1, T2, T3, T4, and T5, respectively. The feeding trial was conducted for 60 days, during which the experimental diets were administered three times daily at 10:00, 14:00, and 18:00H. Shrimp fed the T4 diet showed significantly higher final body weight, weight gain, specific growth rate, protein efficiency ratio, nutrient digestibility, and digestive enzyme activities compared to other treatment groups (P < 0.05). In addition, Shrimp fed the T4 diet (1.20 ± 0.08) exhibited a better feed conversion ratio than the control (1.64 ± 0.06) and other treatment groups. However, survival, whole-body proximate composition, and amino acid profile did not differ significantly among groups (P > 0.05). Following a 14-day challenge test, shrimp fed the T4 diet exhibited significantly higher antioxidant enzyme activities and relative mRNA expression of immune-related genes, including LYZ, TLR, and IMD, compared to the other treatments (P < 0.05). These genes strengthen shrimp innate immunity through antibacterial defence (LYZ), pathogen recognition (TLR), and activation of downstream immune responses (IMD). Furthermore, shrimp in the T4 group exhibited significantly lower cumulative mortality (13.33%) than those in the Control group (53.33%) following infection with Vibrio parahaemolyticus and the pathogen associated with White Feces Syndrome. In conclusion, dietary supplementation with 0.4 g 100 g-1 of the phyto-additive mixture significantly enhanced growth performance, nutrient digestibility and resistance against white feces syndrome in P. vannamei by modulating the innate immunity.

articles.title: Pharmacological and Therapeutic Potential of Garlic (Allium sativum): Integrating Phytochemistry, Molecular Mechanisms, and Clinical and Preclinical Evidence.
articles.abstract: Garlic (Allium sativum) is a medicinal plant with diverse pharmacological properties and therapeutic potential in metabolic, cardiovascular, hepatic, immune, inflammatory, infectious, and neoplastic disorders. However, comprehensive integration of clinical and preclinical evidence remains limited. This review synthesized randomized controlled trials, crossover studies, therapeutic clinical investigations, and experimental animal studies evaluating garlic supplementation. Allicin was identified as the principal intermediate precursor generating numerous bioactive organosulfur compounds. Clinical evidence demonstrated reductions in systolic blood pressure of 5.2%-10.5% and diastolic blood pressure of 4.0%, decreases in LDL cholesterol of 11.8%-14.2% and total cholesterol of 7.6%-14.2%, and increases in HDL cholesterol of 11.5%. Fasting glucose decreased by 7.01 mg/dL, and HbA1c by 0.66%. Inflammatory markers, including TNF-α and C-reactive protein, declined by up to 24.7%, whereas antioxidant capacity increased. Preclinical studies demonstrated reduced tumor growth, improved renal function, enhanced epithelial regeneration, and increased survival in experimental infection models. Garlic demonstrates consistent therapeutic benefits across multiple conditions. Nevertheless, additional high-quality, large-scale clinical trials are required to establish optimal dosing, long-term safety, and clinical efficacy.

articles.title: Medicinal plants vs metronidazole in bacterial vaginosis: a narrative review of evidence from randomized clinical trials.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Bacterial vaginosis (BV) is a common vaginal infection in women of reproductive age and is often linked to a vaginal microbiota imbalance. Conventional antibiotics such as metronidazole are effective but are associated with side effects and recurrence, prompting interest in herbal alternatives. OBJECTIVES: To compare the clinical efficacy of medicinal plants versus metronidazole in the treatment of bacterial vaginosis using evidence from randomized clinical trials. METHODS: This narrative review examined randomized clinical trials evaluating herbal interventions for bacterial vaginosis. Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, and ScienceDirect were searched for studies published up to March 2026. The included studies assessed herbal interventions administered orally or vaginally, alone or with conventional metronidazole therapy. Information on plant species, study design, participants, diagnostic criteria, interventions, results, and conclusions was extracted and synthesized narratively. RESULTS: Twenty-four published articles were included, covering a range of medicinal plants, including Allium sativum, Myrtus communis, Quercus species, Berberis vulgaris, Zataria multiflora, Calendula officinalis, Cymbopogon olivieri, and others. Herbal therapies showed efficacy comparable to or superior to metronidazole, with fewer side effects and lower recurrence rates. Their effects are attributed to bioactive compounds, including allicin, curcumin, berberine, tannins, flavonoids, and essential oils, which exhibit antimicrobial, anti-inflammatory, and antioxidant properties. CONCLUSIONS: Medicinal plants appear to be safe and effective alternatives or adjuncts for bacterial vaginosis; however, the heterogeneity in study designs and short follow-up periods limits definitive conclusions. Further well-designed, multicenter randomized trials with standardized protocols and long-term follow-up, along with studies exploring individual plants and their mechanisms of action, are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and reproducibility and to support evidence-based use.

articles.title: Targeting Alternaria alternata in cheese: Multi-mechanism antifungal activity of essential oils integrating lethal and adaptive stress responses with preliminary olfactory evaluation.
articles.abstract: Mold spoilage is a major challenge in semi-hard cheese production, causing economic losses and quality deterioration. This study evaluated the antifungal activity and mechanisms of essential oils (EOs) from Origanum vulgare (cultivar CARVA) and Thymus vulgaris (cultivar VARICO) against A. alternata isolated from Caciocavallo cheese alongside a preliminary assessment of their olfactory impact. A cheese agar medium (CAM) was developed to mimic the cheese matrix. The MICs of O. vulgare and T. vulgaris EOs were 0.94% and 0.12% (v/v), respectively, and both concentrations prevented fungal growth on inoculated cheese slices during refrigerated storage. T. vulgaris EO showed greater antifungal potency, achieving complete inhibition at a lower concentration than O. vulgare EO in both in vitro and in situ assays. Confocal microscopy showed plasma membrane depolarization, mitochondrial dysfunction, ROS/RNS accumulation, nuclear and structural alterations, and ultimately loss of fungal viability. At sublethal exposure, lipid droplet and chitin accumulation indicated adaptive stress responses. Overall, oregano and thyme EOs acted through a multi-target antifungal mechanism involving membrane disruption, oxidative/nitrosative stress, and cellular damage. Furthermore, a preliminary olfactory evaluation conducted alongside the efficacy trials revealed that high EO concentrations (3.75% and 1.88%) imparted intense herbal aromas and produced greater olfactory alteration relative to the untreated control, whereas treatments at the MIC levels produced comparatively limited olfactory changes. These results suggest that, at the concentrations required for antifungal efficacy, the tested EOs have a detectable olfactory impact, warranting further investigation into their potential application as natural preservatives for hard cheeses.

articles.title: Thyme Beyond Its Traditional Culinary Use: Bioactive Constituents as Potential Modulators of the Gut Microbiome.
articles.journal: Journal of agricultural and food chemistry
articles.abstract: Thyme, particularly Thymus vulgaris L., is a widely used culinary spice and a source of compounds with diverse reported pharmacological activities. This Review examines how thyme extracts, essential oils, and their major constituents, including characteristic monoterpenes, sesquiterpenes, triterpenes, phenolic acids, and flavonoids, interact with the gut microbiome. On the basis of structure-activity relationships, we evaluate how these constituents influence gut microbial composition and function and summarize the implicated mechanisms. Thyme preparations and individual compounds can influence intestinal availability, microbial transformation, and target selectivity, while microbiota-dependent and -independent pathways may contribute to changes in intestinal barrier function, metabolite profiles, and related signaling pathways. Interactions among multiple constituents may produce additive or synergistic effects, suggesting potential advantages of multicomponent thyme preparations, whereas studies of individual compounds can facilitate the target identification and mechanistic analysis. Future research should systematically address gaps in causal validation, formulation standardization, and human evidence to consolidate the translational foundations.

articles.title: Essential oils for acute cystitis: a real-world experience in primary care settings.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute cystitis is a significant public health challenge, with escalating antimicrobial: resistance threatening conventional antibiotic therapy. Essential oils (EOs) containing bioactive compounds such as carvacrol and cinnamaldehyde, offer multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms that may provide effective alternatives while supporting antimicrobial stewardship efforts. METHODS: This real-world observational study compared the clinical efficacy of an EO-based formulation with that of standard antibiotic therapy in women with acute cystitis. 68 patients participated: Groups A (N.=24), treated with fosfomycin trometamol 3 g single-dose; Group B (N.=21) received the EO combination (OLEOBIOTIC® Salud urinaria manufactured by Pranarom International S.A.) at the standard dose (1 capsule 3 times daily for 5 days); Group C (N.=23) received the double dosage. OLEOBIOTIC® Salud urinaria is a food supplement manufactured by Pranarom International S.A. and formulated with EOs of oregano (Origanum vulgare) 10 mg, Chinese cinnamon (Cinnamomum cassia) 30 mg, lemon (Citrus limon) 5 mg, lemongrass (Cymbopogon citratus) 40 mg, thyme (Thymus vulgaris, thymol chemotype) 20 mg, savory (Satureja montana) 20 mg, cloves (Caryophyllus aromaticus) 10 mg, and fennel (Foeniculum vulgare) 15 mg. Primary outcomes was urinary dipstick test negativization. Secondary outcomes assessed symptom severity, patient satisfaction, antibiotic avoidance, and safety profile. RESULTS: Urinary dipstick negativization rates were comparable across groups: Group A 83.3%, Group B 90.5%, and Group C 78.3% (P>0.05). All groups showed a significant improvement in urinary frequency (P<0.001), with patients urinating ≤4 times daily increasing from baseline to post-treatment: Group A from 25.0% to 70.8%, Group B from 19.0% to 85.7%, and Group C from 21.7% to 69.6%. Antibiotic prescription was avoided in 66.7-78.3% of cases. Patient satisfaction was high across all groups, with 71.4% to 100% willing to use the treatment again. Only one adverse event (self-limiting diarrhea) was reported, with no recurrences during follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: EO-based formulations demonstrated clinically significant efficacy in the managing of acute cystitis, with high dipstick negativization rates, substantial symptom relief, and excellent safety profile. The multi-target antimicrobial mechanisms of key components offer theoretical advantages for reducing the development of resistance. These findings may support integrating natural treatments into clinical algorithms for uncomplicated cystitis as part of comprehensive antimicrobial stewardship strategies. Nevertheless, randomized controlled trials are needed to confirm these real-world observations.

articles.title: Functional enhancement of fermented dairy-based tarhana with Thymus vulgaris: phytochemical characterisation and in vitro antidiabetic potential.
articles.journal: Journal of the science of food and agriculture
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: This study investigated the effects of Thymus vulgaris (TV) enrichment on the phytochemical profile, antioxidant capacity, antimicrobial activity, amino acid composition, and α-glucosidase inhibitory potential of fermented dairy-based tarhana. Tarhana was produced in three formulations (control, 40 g kg-1 (TV4), and 80 g kg-1 (TV8) thyme enrichment) under controlled fermentation and drying conditions. RESULTS: The results showed that TV integration significantly increased total phenolic content (TPC) and total flavonoid content (TFC) in a dose-dependent manner, leading to superior DPPH and ABTS radical scavenging activities. Microbiological analysis revealed a selective antimicrobial effect; TV effectively suppressed yeast and mould growth while maintaining the viability of lactic acid bacteria (LAB), ensuring fermentation integrity. Specifically, TV enrichment increased nutrient density, raising total free amino acids from 1821.7 μg g-1 to 2803.6 μg g-1. Liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) analysis identified a robust bioactive profile, including rosmarinic acid, luteolin, and naringenin. The TV8 group exhibited a strong antidiabetic profile, providing approximately 90% inhibition of α-glucosidase. Molecular docking confirmed that TV-derived ligands exhibited high binding affinities in the catalytic pockets of metabolic enzymes, mimicking or exceeding the stability of standard inhibitors. CONCLUSION: The results demonstrate that thyme enrichment enhances the functional and bioactive properties of fermented dairy-based tarhana, offering a scientifically supported strategy for developing value-added functional dairy products with potential metabolic health benefits. © 2026 Society of Chemical Industry.

articles.title: Chitosan/Tripolyphosphate Nanoparticles Encapsulating Essential Oils as a New Class of Biopesticides: Structural Properties and Ecotoxicity Evaluation.
articles.abstract: Essential oils (EO) are fragrant, hydrophobic natural products derived from aromatic and medicinal plants that can be highly sensitive to environmental conditions. Nanoencapsulation offers a promising solution to overcome environmental degradation by abiotic factors. In this work, ionic gelation was employed to synthesize formulations of EO extracted from Satureja montana , Thymus vulgaris , Anethum graveolens , and Coriandrum sativum encapsulated in chitosan/TPP (tripolyphosphate) nanoparticles. Despite their potential as biopesticides, ecotoxicological aspects have not been much explored. Herein, aquatic (Aliivibrio fisheri, Raphidocelis subcapitata, Lemna minor , and Daphnia magna ) and terrestrial ( Folsomia candida and soil microbial activity) non-target organisms were used to assess the environmental impact of the EO encapsulated in chitosan/TPP nanoparticles. The chitosan nanoparticles had a positive charge, high homogeneity (PDI < 0.2), an average size of about 200 nm, and showed encapsulation efficiencies between 82% and 98%. Regarding hazard assessment, EO in their free form can cause toxic effects, even though they are prone to degradation by environmental factors. Encapsulation into chitosan/TPP nanoparticles resulted in a significant reduction of the essential oils' toxic profile. Overall, the observed toxicity comes mainly from the EO activity toward the aquatic test species. By reducing the ecotoxicity of EO toward non-target species (except for collembolans), the nanoformulations proved a promising solution to be explored as biopesticides, aiming to replace the use of synthetic pesticides. Only the nanoencapsulated C. sativum EO caused an inhibitory effect on nitrogen mineralization and arylsulfatase activity. Moreover, enhancing our understanding of the ecotoxicological impact of nanobiopesticides is essential before recommending their use in crop protection.

articles.title: Elemental composition of the three poisonous Digitalis L. species of Moldovan origin determined by instrumental neutron activation analysis.
articles.abstract: Digitalis species play a significant role in the treatment of congestive heart failure and other cardiac diseases. Instrumental neutron activation analysis was employed to determine the elemental composition of three species: Digitalis ferruginea L., Digitalis lanata Ehrh., and Digitalis purpurea L. (n = 9). Analytical quality was assured using certified reference materials. Among the major elements, potassium exhibited the highest mass fractions, with values ranging from 1.52 ± 0.1% in D. purpurea to 2.79 ± 0.2% in D. ferruginea. Chlorine and iron were identified as the most abundant minor elements. Among potentially toxic elements, arsenic was detected in Digitalis ferruginea and Digitalis purpurea, whereas antimony and other elements were determiend in all species. The range of elements quantified in the present study considerably exceeds that reported in previous investigations on other Digitalis species. Notably, the mass fractions of nearly all determined elements were found to be higher in D. purpurea, which may be attributed to its biological properties and high metal uptake capacity-a finding that warrants further investigation.

articles.title: Engineering of plant-derived P450scc for de novo biosynthesis of pregnenolone.
articles.abstract: In contrast to the extensively researched animal CYP11A1 system, the catalytic mechanism of sterol side-chain cleavage by plant-derived cytochrome P450scc enzymes remains poorly understood. Through the integration of computational structural biology and enzyme channel engineering, this study successfully elucidated the key intermediates in the stepwise hydroxylation-cleavage catalytic process of Digitalis purpurea-derived DlCYP87A enzyme. Building on this foundation, we implemented structure-guided rational design to precisely engineer the substrate channel and catalytic pocket, systematically delineating their structure-activity relationships, which ultimately overcame the critical catalytic bottleneck of low conversion efficiency in heterologous microbial systems expressing plant-derived P450scc. This study established an efficient steroid synthesis system in Saccharomyces cerevisiae through integrated systematic enzyme engineering and transcriptome-guided organelle optimization. In a 5-liter fermentation system, engineered strain P4 achieved a pregnenolone titer of 1.46 g/L. This achievement represents the first gram-scale breakthrough in de novo pregnenolone biosynthesis, laying a crucial technological foundation for scalable bio-manufacturing of steroid precursors and pioneering a new industrial production pathway.

articles.title: Genome sequence of the ornamental plant Digitalis purpurea reveals the molecular basis of flower color and morphology variation.
articles.abstract: Digitalis purpurea (foxglove) is a widely distributed ornamental plant. Here, we present a long read sequencing-based genome sequence of a magenta flowering D. purpurea plant and a corresponding prediction of gene models. The high assembly continuity is indicated by the N50 of 4.3 Mbp and the completeness is supported by discovery of about 96% complete BUSCO genes. This genomic resource paves the way for an in-depth investigation of the flower pigmentation of D. purpurea. Structural genes of the anthocyanin biosynthesis and the corresponding transcriptional regulators were identified. The comparison of magenta and white flowering plants revealed a large insertion in the anthocyanidin synthase gene in white flowering plants that most likely renders this gene non-functional and could explain the loss of anthocyanin pigmentation. Furthermore, we found a large insertion in the DpTFL1/CEN gene to be likely responsible for the development of large terminal flowers.

articles.title: Flower color variation in Digitalis purpurea: Pollination and soil influences across native and introduced populations.
articles.abstract: PREMISE: Flower color, a key trait influencing plant-pollinator interactions, may be influenced by abiotic factors such as soil. We investigated association between pollinators, soil characteristics, and flower color variations in Digitalis purpurea across native populations in Sweden and introduced populations in Bolivia. METHODS: We measured floral traits, reflectance of petals and nectar-guide spots, plant size, pollinator visitation, fruit set, seed production, germination, and soil characteristics. RESULTS: Individuals were categorized into violet, pink, and white morphs, which were confirmed by spectral measurements and bee vision modelling. Reflectance of inner nectar-guide spots overlapped across morphs, potentially limiting pollinator discrimination. Bumblebees were the main pollinators in all populations. Although visitation varied among morphs, pollinator visits to different color morphs were population specific. In Bolivia, violet flowers were predominant (70-87%), with pink (13-17%) and white (0-13%) at lower frequencies. In Sweden, morph frequencies were more even (violet 20-43%, pink 38-69%, white 11-30%). Morph frequency was not associated with soil composition, despite differences between regions. Reproductive fitness varied across populations but not consistently among morphs: The largest Swedish population had the highest fruit set but the lowest seed set, while germination was lower in Bolivia. Phosphorus was lower in soil beneath violet individuals; other soil variables, plant size, and floral traits did not differ among color morphs. CONCLUSIONS: Floral color variation in D. purpurea was not significantly related to pollinator visitation or soil conditions at the spatial scale examined, suggesting maintenance by local environmental conditions, neutrality, or historical and demographic processes rather than selection.

articles.title: Medicinal plants and functional foods with diuretic effects: a nutraceutical approach to cardiovascular health.
articles.abstract: Fluid and electrolyte balance is essential for cardiovascular homeostasis, and disturbances in renal sodium and water handling contribute to hypertension, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease. Although pharmacological diuretics remain a cornerstone of therapy, their long-term use may be limited by electrolyte disturbances, neurohormonal activation, and reduced tolerability in frail or polymedicated patients. This narrative review examines current experimental and clinical evidence on medicinal plants and functional foods with mild diuretic or renal-vascular effects, highlighting their potential role as adjunctive strategies. Several botanicals, including Hibiscus sabdariffa, Orthosiphon stamineus, Urtica dioica, and Taraxacum officinale, exhibit natriuretic, aquaretic, antioxidant, and vasorelaxant properties through multifactorial mechanisms. However, clinical evidence remains limited, heterogeneous, and frequently derived from multicomponent formulations, hindering the attribution of specific effects. In addition, dietary sources such as potassium-rich foods, herbal infusions, and whole grains may modulate fluid balance and vascular function. Still, their interaction with standard diuretic therapy warrants careful consideration. Potential nutrient-drug interactions may result in either synergistic effects or adverse outcomes, including hyperkalaemia, dehydration, or altered drug absorption. Overall, selected medicinal plants and functional foods may provide supportive benefits in early-stage cardiovascular and metabolic conditions. Still, their clinical use should remain adjunctive and individualized, pending further standardized, well-designed clinical trials.

articles.title: Experimental and DFT Investigation of Crystal Violet Biosorption by Taraxacum officinale Leaf Biomass.
articles.abstract: Leaf powder obtained from wild Taraxacum officinale was directly used as a biosorbent for the removal of Crystal Violet (CV), a widely used cationic dye, because the leaves are rich in fibers and minerals and have not previously been employed in their untreated form for biosorption. Standard instrumental analyses were employed for the identification of surface functional groups (FT-IR), imaging of surface morphology (FE-SEM), and elemental characterization (EDX). Adsorption was favored under alkaline conditions, reaching a maximum removal efficiency of 46.53% at pH 12, corresponding to an experimental adsorption capacity of 149.1 mg g-1, while adsorbent dosages between 100 and 200 mg were effective for dye removal. The untreated biomass surface exhibited adsorption-favoring grooves and stomata. Taraxacum officinale biomass exhibited a lignocellulosic structure, with carbon and oxygen contents of 54.26 and 42.46 at%, respectively. Adsorption equilibrium was best described by the nonlinear Langmuir model (R 2 = 0.948), supporting monolayer adsorption onto a relatively homogeneous surface. The D-R model further supported a physicochemical adsorption mechanism. Frontier molecular orbital (FMO) and natural bond orbital (NBO) analyses were performed at the B3LYP/6-311++G** level in both gas and aqueous media to elucidate the electronic interactions between CV and the lignocellulosic surface.

articles.title: Multielement Composition and in Vitro Bioaccessibility in Brazilian Edible Floral Supplement Capsules Containing Dandelion and Hibiscus.
articles.abstract: Dandelion (Taraxacum officinale) and hibiscus (Hibiscus sabdariffa) are notable unconventional edible flowers (UEFs) that have traditionally been used as food and in herbal preparations. This study examined the in vitro bioaccessibility content of six elements (Cr, Cu, Fe, Mn, Ni, and Zn) in edible flower capsules sold in Brazil. Acid digestion in a closed system and microwave-induced plasma optical emission spectrometry (MIP OES) were employed, as well as simulated gastrointestinal digestion according to the INFOGEST 2.0 in vitro protocol. Additionally, we examined the contribution of the in vitro bioaccessible fraction (FBio) in relation to the recommended daily intake (RDI). The concentrations (in µg g⁻1) of the target elements were as follows: Cr (< 0.46-2.82), Cu (< 0.48-11.45), Fe (159.44-1880.90), Mn (48.94-441.34), Ni (< 0.44-3.21), and Zn (< 0.55-30.98). The FBio of the evaluated elements ranged from 0.13% to 14.31%. Although Fe had high total levels, its bioaccessibility was limited, contributing only 0.13%. In contrast, Mn and Ni exhibited high gastrointestinal release, accounting for 12.13% and 14.31% of the FBio, respectively. Mn showed high gastrointestinal release, providing up to 209.3% of the RDI. This study is the first to specifically evaluate the bioaccessible trace element content of these edible flowers using the INFOGEST 2.0 in vitro protocol and MIP OES to assess microelements. Overall, the results highlight the importance of incorporating chemical composition and bioaccessibility data into the multi-element characterization of dandelion and hibiscus.

articles.title: Integrative Approaches in Cardiovascular Disease: The Role of Nutraceuticals in Heart Failure, Atrial Fibrillation, and Related Conditions.
articles.abstract: Heart failure (HF) and atrial fibrillation (AF) are among the most prevalent cardiovascular diseases, often coexisting and sharing common pathophysiological pathways such as systemic inflammation, oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, and endothelial impairment. Despite substantial progress in pharmacological treatment, including renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) inhibitors, beta-blockers, sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 (SGLT2) inhibitors, mineralocorticoid receptor antagonists (MRAs), diuretics, and antiarrhythmic drugs, many patients continue to experience residual symptoms and drug-related adverse effects. Nutraceuticals have emerged as potential adjuncts to conventional therapy due to their ability to modulate key biological processes involved in HF and AF. Polyphenols from Olea europaea , Hibiscus sabdariffa , Camellia sinensis , and Vitis vinifera (resveratrol) exhibit antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and vasoprotective effects. Omega-3 fatty acids and astaxanthin contribute to inflammation control and redox balance, while Orthosiphon stamineus and Taraxacum officinale show mild diuretic activity. Moreover, anthocyanins, ursolic acid, and Rhodiola crenulata may exert antifibrotic and antiarrhythmic properties. This review provides a mechanistic comparison between pharmacological agents and nutraceuticals with overlapping mechanisms of action, highlighting their potential role in integrative cardiovascular care. While nutraceuticals are not substitutes for established therapies, emerging evidence supports their complementary use in improving treatment response, reducing side effects, and enhancing patient outcomes. Future research should focus on large-scale trials, improved bioavailability, standardized formulations, and the development of personalized therapeutic strategies. Challenges related to dosage consistency, clinical validation, and regulatory oversight are also addressed to guide innovation in integrative cardiology.

articles.title: Analysis of Mercury Content in Medicinal Plants Popular in Poland.
articles.abstract: The use of herbal medicinal products and dietary supplements has increased significantly in recent years. Insufficient knowledge regarding the effects of herbal raw materials, as well as their potential adverse effects and interactions with medications and food, poses a considerable risk in therapies involving these products. Furthermore, contamination with heavy metals, including mercury, may constitute an additional health hazard. The aim of this study was to determine the mercury (Hg) content in wild-growing herbal raw materials collected independently and in commercial products, namely herbal teas derived from the same plant species under investigation. The measured Hg levels were compared with the limits established by the applicable standard set out in Commission Regulation (EU) 2018/73. For the study, five medicinal plant species commonly used in Poland were selected: wild rose (Rosa canina L.), common hawthorn (Crataegus monogyna L.), dandelion (Taraxacum officinale), common nettle (Urtica dioica L.) and silver birch (Betula pendula). The determination of Hg concentrations was carried out using an AMA 254 (Altec, Prague, Czech Republic) atomic absorption spectrometer. The arithmetic mean Hg concentration across all analyzed samples was 18.68 µg/kg, with values ranging from 0.19 to 202.83 µg/kg. The highest median Hg concentrations were found in common nettle (23.80 µg/kg), followed by dandelion (13.00 µg/kg) and silver birch (12.68 µg/kg). Considerably lower concentrations were observed in common hawthorn (5.91 µg/kg) and wild rose (0.61 µg/kg). Statistically significant differences in Hg content were detected among the studied plant species (p < 0.001). With regard to individual morphological plant parts, the highest accumulation of Hg was observed in roots, followed by herbs, leaves, and buds. Among all analyzed samples, 32% exceeded the permissible Hg limit, with the majority of these being self-collected samples. Self-collection of medicinal plant materials, including common nettle (Urtica dioica), dandelion (Taraxacum officinale), and silver birch (Betula pendula), may pose a risk associated with Hg contamination. Given the continuously increasing demand for and market value of herbal medicines, ensuring the safety, quality, and efficacy of medicinal plants and herbal products is of great importance. Therefore, regular monitoring of toxic element levels in plant materials used in phytotherapy is justified and essential.

articles.title: Herb-drug interactions with clinical impact: A systematic review of global clinical evidence on medicinal plants widely used in Ecuador.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: The widespread use of medicinal plants in Ecuador increases the risk of herb-drug interactions, many of which may compromise patient safety. Understanding clinically relevant interactions is essential for preventing adverse events and guiding evidence-based decision-making. AIM OF THE STUDY: To systematically analyze the clinical evidence on interactions between medicinal plants commonly used in Ecuador and conventional medications, identifying their mechanisms and potential therapeutic risks. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Articles published between 2015 and 2025 were retrieved from major scientific databases. Studies involving humans and reporting herb-drug interactions were included. Studies conducted worldwide involving medicinal plants commonly used in Ecuador were considered. Methodological quality was assessed using predefined indicators, and interactions were classified according to the Janusmed clinical interaction severity scale. RESULTS: Out of 102 records, 47 studies met inclusion criteria. Among these, 31.9% reported clinically relevant interactions. The most frequent consequences were reduced plasma drug levels (40%), increased risk of bleeding (13.3%), decreased efficacy of immunotherapy (13.3%), and hepatotoxic or endocrine effects. The most frequently implicated plants were Camellia sinensis L., Hypericum perforatum L., Borago officinalis, and Glycyrrhiza glabra L. CONCLUSIONS: Clinically significant herb-drug interactions are common among medicinal plants widely used in Ecuador and may affect therapeutic efficacy or increase adverse effects. Greater awareness among healthcare professionals is essential to improve patient safety and prevent harmful combinations.

articles.title: Auxin interacts with kynurenine metabolism during organogenesis in Hypericum perforatum L.
articles.journal: Plant science : an international journal of experimental plant biology
articles.abstract: Recent studies have demonstrated the presence of kynurenine (KYN) and kynurenic acid (KYNA) in several plant species, but their function in plant growth and metabolism remains undefined. We hypothesized that KYN and KYNA are metabolites of auxin and play a role in plant morphogenesis. To test our hypothesis, we developed a plant tissue-culture-based bioassay using Hypericum perforatum (St. John's wort; SJW), a model system for auxin and indoleamine metabolism which uses exogenous treatment with IAA, KYN or pharmacological inhibitors of KYN metabolism in humans (PF- 04859989, PF; RO -61-8048, RO or JM6) to investigate both morphogenetic and metabolic responses of kynurenine metabolism in planta. 10 μM KYN supplementation increased root number and internodal length relative to control, and increased concentrations of downstream metabolites KYN, KYNA, and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid (3-HAA) in both roots and shoots. Application of the inhibitors JM6 and PF which targets KYN monooxygenase (KMO) and KYN aminotransferase, respectively, lead to an increase in the pool of KYN present in tissues, but did not significantly reduce KYNA or 3-HAA. To investigate interactions between auxin and KYN, treatment with exogenously applied IAA with or without the inhibitors was also evaluated. IAA alone, significantly increased KYN and 3-HAA in explants. Co-application of JM6 and IAA partially recovered root organogenesis in explants. IAA + JM6 co-treatment also lead to the highest KYN accumulation in tissues, supporting an interaction between the pathways. Together, these data propose a role for KYN in IAA metabolism, shoot and root organogenesis.

articles.title: Hypericum perforatum L.: A legacy of herbal medicine in light of modern scientific evidence.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Hypericum perforatum L. has been used for centuries in traditional medicine, with core therapeutic applications including alleviation of emotional, wound and burn healing and neurological disorders, and antiparasitic treatments. AIM OF THE STUDY: This review summarizes and interprets current knowledge on the traditional use, phytochemistry, pharmacology, quality control, safety, and herb-drug interactions of H. perforatum, with particular attention to the relationships between major constituents, proposed mechanisms, and clinical relevance. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Relevant literature on H. perforatum was identified through major scientific databases, including CNKI, Web of Science, and PubMed, together with complementary sources such as Flora of China, classical herbal literature, and academic dissertations. RESULTS: H. perforatum contains diverse bioactive constituents, notably PPAPs, naphthodianthrones, and flavonoids. The strongest clinical evidence supports its use in mild-to-moderate depression and menopausal symptoms, with efficacy comparable to SSRIs and superiority over placebo. Preliminary case reports also suggest potential benefits in diabetic complications, though these findings are limited. Beyond depression, most pharmacological activities, including neuroprotective, anticancer, antiviral, antimicrobial, wound healing, and metabolic effects, remain preclinical. Recent advances in nanoformulation strategies (e.g., nanostructured lipid carriers, plant-derived exosome-like nanovesicles) have enhanced the performance of key constituents such as hypericin and hyperforin in photodynamic therapy and antimicrobial applications. Quality control has evolved from single-marker assays to holistic approaches integrating non-targeted metabolomics, machine learning, and fingerprinting, addressing compositional variability and heavy metal contamination. However, heterogeneity in plant material, extraction procedures, constituent standardization, and experimental design still complicates data interpretation. Clinically relevant herb-drug interactions, especially those associated with CYP enzyme and P-gp induction, remain a major safety concern. CONCLUSION: This narrative review indicates that H. perforatum has established efficacy in depression and broader but uneven pharmacological potential elsewhere. Emerging formulation technologies and multi-component quality control offer promising ways to improve consistency and efficacy. Future progress requires better extract standardization, clearer constituent-mechanism links, higher-quality clinical trials (especially for non-psychiatric uses), and continued attention to safety and drug interactions.

articles.title: The role of kynurenine in thidiazuron-induced morphogenesis in St. John's wort (Hypericum perforatum L.).
articles.abstract: Kynurenine (KYN) is produced by catabolism of IAA and tryptophan. Our data indicate that thidiazuron reduces KYN levels during the expression phase of de-novo shoot organogenesis. Thidiazuron [TDZ; 1-phenyl-3-(1,2,3-thiadiazol-5-yl)urea] is a synthetic herbicide and plant growth regulator (PGR) commonly used to induce regeneration in plant tissue cultures. The exact mechanisms of action of TDZ remain to be discovered. We hypothesized that TDZ mediates shikimic acid metabolism and developed a model bioassay using TDZ-induced de novo shoot organogenesis on St. John's wort nodal explants for these investigations. TDZ-induced formation of compact callus at the cut surface of stem explants and de novo shoots at the terminal end of shoot vascular midribs. Kynurenine (KYN) is the primary catabolic product of tryptophan oxidation and has been proposed as a product of auxin catabolism. The current study investigated the effects of TDZ on KYN metabolism using the KYN aminotransferase inhibitor PF-04859989 and KYN oxygenase inhibitors RO-61-8048 and JM6. TDZ significantly decreased KYN in St. John's wort explants after 35 days of culture. Statistically significant differences were not observed in serotonin, melatonin or indole-3-acetic acid but a non-significant decrease in serotonin in TDZ-exposed explants was noted. Together, these data indicate a possible mechanism of TDZ activity through inhibition of the catabolism of tryptophan and/or auxin.

articles.title: Treatment of the Subacute Phase of Spinal Cord Injury in Rats by Hypericin and Hypericum perforatum L. Extract: Evaluation of Oxidative Stress, Neurotrophic Factors, and Remyelination.
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Spinal Cord Injury (SCI) is a serious clinical problem that often leads to spinal cord destruction and is associated with varying degrees of sensory and motor dysfunction. Oxidative stress is a hallmark of SCI; therefore, mitigating it could be considered a therapeutic intervention. Hypericum perforatum L. possesses numerous properties, including antioxidant and neuroprotective effects. The use of hypericin (one of the most important compounds of Hypericum perforatum L.) and Hypericum extract may effectively reduce oxidative stress and subsequent inflammation. This study compared the effects of hypericin and Hypericum extract on oxidative stress, neurotrophic factors, and remyelination in a rat contusion model of SCI during the subacute phase. METHODS: In this study, Hypericum extract was first obtained by Soxhlet extraction. For the animal study, 42 adult female Wistar rats were randomly allocated into seven groups (n=6): healthy control, sham (laminectomy), injury (SCI), injury + hypericin 50 mg/kg, injury + hypericin 100 mg/kg, injury + Hypericum extract 50 mg/kg, and injury + Hypericum extract 100 mg/kg. SCI was induced at the T8 spinal segment by applying a clip for 1 minute. One week post-injury, treatment with hypericin or Hypericum extract at doses of 50 or 100 mg/kg was administered daily via gavage for one week. At the end of the study, blood was drawn from the animals' hearts to measure oxidative stress markers (NO, ROS) and neurotrophic factors (BDNF, NGF) using the ELISA method. The studied spinal segment was then extracted, processed for histology, and sectioned at 5μm thickness for Luxol Fast Blue (LFB) staining. Functional recovery was assessed weekly using the Basso, Beattie, Bresnahan (BBB) locomotor rating scale. RESULTS: The results demonstrated that both hypericin and Hypericum extract dose-dependently reduced oxidative stress (ROS, NO), decreased NGF levels, and increased BDNF levels. However, the magnitude of these effects was greater in the hypericin-treated groups compared to the Hypericum extracttreated groups. The findings from the motor function tests and LFB Staining confirmed these results. DISCUSSION: The superior efficacy of purified hypericin over the Hypericum extract suggests that hypericin may be a key active constituent; however, the dose-equivalence issue and the presence of other bioactive compounds limit the conclusion that hypericin is solely responsible. Therefore, standardizing treatments based on hypericin content rather than total Hypericum extract could lead to more predictable and potent clinical outcomes for SCI. CONCLUSION: The findings of the present study indicate that both hypericin and Hypericum extract positively impact oxidative stress and neurotrophic factors (BDNF, NGF). Since reducing oxidative stress and favorably modulating neurotrophic factors are considered beneficial therapeutic interventions for SCI, the Hypericum extract, particularly hypericin, could be proposed as a promising candidate for the treatment of spinal cord injury.

articles.title: Mechanism and active ingredients of Gancao Qinlian Granules in ameliorating ulcerative colitis:integrated in vivo, in vitro, network pharmacology and untargeted metabolomics investigation.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: Gancao Qinlian Granules (GQG) are a granulated formulation of the classical prescription Gancao Xiexin Tang, originally documented by Zhang Zhongjing in the Treatise on Febrile and Miscellaneous Diseases (Shang Han Za Bing Lun, c. 220 CE). This formula comprises six medicinal components: Glycyrrhiza glabra L. (Gancao), the radix of Scutellaria baicalensis Georgi (Huangqin), Ziziphus jujuba Mill. (Dazao), the rhizomes of Zingiber officinale Roscoe (Ganjiang), the dried tuber of Pinellia ternata (Thunb.) Breit (Banxia), and the rhizoma of Coptis chinensis Franch (Huanglian). GQG has been extensively employed in traditional and contemporary clinical practice for the treatment of ulcerative colitis (UC). Nevertheless, its candidate bioactive constituents and underlying mechanisms of action remain incompletely elucidated. AIM OF THE STUDY: To comprehensively characterize the chemical composition of GQG and elucidate its therapeutic mechanisms against UC through an integrated strategy combining network pharmacology prediction, serum/colon/fecal multi-omics profiling (metabolomics and microbiome), and experimental validation. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Initially, GQG was analyzed by UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap MS under negative/positive ion modes, with compound identification via mzCloud, HMDB, and literature matching. C57BL/6 mice (n = 8/group) were induced with UC using 3% dextran sulfate sodium (DSS) for 15 days. UC-related targets from GeneCard, PharmGkb, TTD, and OMIM were integrated to construct compound-target-pathway networks (Cytoscape 3.10.1). Secondly, GQG (9 g/kg/d, 12 g/kg/d, 15 g/kg/d) or mesalazine (300 mg/kg) was administered orally for 10 days. Disease severity was assessed daily via Disease Activity Index (DAI: weight loss, stool consistency, bleeding). Post-euthanasia, colon length was measured, and histopathology (H&E, Alcian Blue-Periodic Acid Schiff staining) analyzed mucosal damage and goblet cell depletion. Colon IL-1β levels were quantified by immunohistochemistry (IHC). Then, serum, fecal, and colonic tissue samples underwent UHPLC-Q-Exactive Orbitrap MS-based untargeted metabolomics. Differentially expressed metabolites (DEMs) were identified (VIP >1, p < 0.05) and pathways enriched via KEGG. Fecal 16S rDNA sequencing (Illumina NovaSeq) analyzed microbial α/β-diversity and differential taxa (LEfSe, LDA score >3). Subsequently, Integrated component analysis, network pharmacology, and metabolomics data to obtain the mechanism by which GQG improves UC, and verify the related target proteins through IHC and Western blot. Finally, obtain the candidate bioactive constituents in GQG through molecular docking, and verify the efficacy of these bioactive constituents with their targets on a cellular model. RESULTS: Chemical profiling revealed 121 constituents in GQG, with 53 flavonoids (43.8%) including core bioactive markers (e.g., licoflavone B, licuroside). In DSS-induced ulcerative colitis mice, GQG (12 g/kg/d) exerted potent therapeutic effects: reducing disease activity index, attenuating colon shortening, restoring goblet cells, and suppressing colon IL-1β. Mechanistically, GQG remodeled gut microbiota composition and function, increasing beneficial taxa (Muribaculaceae, Lactobacillus). This microbiota restructuring directly drove metabolic reprogramming. Suppression of pro-inflammatory metabolism: purine degradation (hypoxanthine), tryptophan-derived uremic toxins (kynurenine), pathogenic bile acids (deoxycholic acid). Integrative analysis of the microbiota-metabolite axis reveals that GQG extract can regulate the NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome cascade through p-NF-κB p65 expression, NLRP3 assembly (NLRP3, Caspase-1), and ASC speck formation. Combined with molecular docking, six key components in GQG exhibit high affinity for critical targets. In vitro cellular experiments demonstrate that these core candidate bioactive components effectively inhibit key targets within the target pathway. CONCLUSIONS: GQG ameliorates UC by modulating gut microbiota structure and function, restoring microbial co-metabolism (e.g., SCFA synthesis, bile acid homeostasis), and subsequently inhibiting the NF-κB/NLRP3 inflammasome axis. This integrated approach substantiates the ethnopharmacological application of GQG for UC.

articles.title: Herb-drug interactions with clinical impact: A systematic review of global clinical evidence on medicinal plants widely used in Ecuador.
articles.abstract: ETHNOPHARMACOLOGICAL RELEVANCE: The widespread use of medicinal plants in Ecuador increases the risk of herb-drug interactions, many of which may compromise patient safety. Understanding clinically relevant interactions is essential for preventing adverse events and guiding evidence-based decision-making. AIM OF THE STUDY: To systematically analyze the clinical evidence on interactions between medicinal plants commonly used in Ecuador and conventional medications, identifying their mechanisms and potential therapeutic risks. MATERIALS AND METHODS: A systematic review was conducted following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. Articles published between 2015 and 2025 were retrieved from major scientific databases. Studies involving humans and reporting herb-drug interactions were included. Studies conducted worldwide involving medicinal plants commonly used in Ecuador were considered. Methodological quality was assessed using predefined indicators, and interactions were classified according to the Janusmed clinical interaction severity scale. RESULTS: Out of 102 records, 47 studies met inclusion criteria. Among these, 31.9% reported clinically relevant interactions. The most frequent consequences were reduced plasma drug levels (40%), increased risk of bleeding (13.3%), decreased efficacy of immunotherapy (13.3%), and hepatotoxic or endocrine effects. The most frequently implicated plants were Camellia sinensis L., Hypericum perforatum L., Borago officinalis, and Glycyrrhiza glabra L. CONCLUSIONS: Clinically significant herb-drug interactions are common among medicinal plants widely used in Ecuador and may affect therapeutic efficacy or increase adverse effects. Greater awareness among healthcare professionals is essential to improve patient safety and prevent harmful combinations.

articles.title: Glycyrrhizic acid alters [99mTc]Tc-PSMA biodistribution and tumour progression in a DMBA-induced breast cancer model.
articles.journal: European journal of pharmaceutical sciences : official journal of the European Federation for Pharmaceutical Sciences
articles.abstract: Breast cancer remains a major global health challenge, and understanding interactions between pharmacological agents and radiopharmaceuticals is important for interpreting molecular imaging findings. Glycyrrhizic acid (GA), a bioactive triterpenoid derived from Glycyrrhiza glabra, has reported anti-inflammatory and anticancer activities; however, its effects on PSMA-targeted radiotracer biodistribution remain poorly investigated. This study evaluated GA effects on tumour-related biological responses and [99mTc]Tc-PSMA biodistribution in vitro and in vivo. Cytotoxicity, migration, and invasion were assessed in MDA-MB-231 breast cancer cells. Cell-free PSMA enzyme kinetics and a separate cellular [99mTc]Tc-PSMA uptake assay were performed to distinguish effects on PSMA enzymatic activity from cell-associated radiotracer uptake. In vivo studies used a DMBA-induced mammary tumour model in female Sprague-Dawley rats, followed by SPECT/CT imaging and tissue biodistribution analysis. GA reduced cell viability concentration-dependently (IC₅₀ = 20 µM at 48 h) and suppressed migration and invasion. Cell-free kinetic analysis showed an apparent non-competitive PSMA inhibition pattern (Ki = 12.4 ± 1.5 µM), although this does not establish the molecular binding site. In vivo, GA reduced tumour uptake of [99mTc]Tc-PSMA by 57% (P < 0.005) and altered non-target tissue distribution. Despite reduced absolute tumour uptake, the tumour-to-background ratio increased because background activity decreased proportionally more. GA was also associated with reduced tumour growth and metastatic burden and altered inflammatory, angiogenic, and apoptotic markers. Overall, GA alters tumour biology and [99mTc]Tc-PSMA biodistribution, while the mechanism underlying radiotracer changes remains unresolved.

articles.title: Phytochemical profiling, antimicrobial, cytotoxic and apoptotic effects of Glycyrrhiza glabra ethanolic extract.
articles.journal: Zeitschrift fur Naturforschung. C, Journal of biosciences
articles.abstract: Glycyrrhiza glabra L. is a medicinal plant rich in bioactive compounds, yet detailed studies on its antimicrobial, cytotoxic, and apoptotic properties remain limited. This research evaluated these effects using an ethanolic extract of G. glabra. The extract was prepared via Soxhlet extraction, and its chemical constituents were identified using gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS). In vitro antimicrobial activity was tested against various microorganisms through well diffusion and microdilution methods, while minimum bactericidal and fungicidal concentrations were determined using agar plate assays. Cytotoxicity on HepG2 human hepatocellular carcinoma cells was assessed with the MTT assay. Additionally, the expression of apoptosis-related genes (p53, Bax, and Bcl-2) was analyzed by quantitative real-time PCR. GC-MS results revealed a total of 28 compounds, with 2,8-dimethyl-7,8-dihydro-6H-cyclohepta (18.59 %) and thiophene (16.58 %) as the major constituents. The extract showed strong antimicrobial effects, especially against Gram-positive bacteria such as Listeria monocytogenes, Enterococcus faecalis, and Streptococcus mutans. Among Gram-negative strains, Salmonella enteritidis was the most susceptible. Cytotoxic activity against HepG2 cells was observed, with an IC50 value of 206.8 µg/mL. This effect was associated with increased expression of p53 and Bax and decreased Bcl-2 levels, indicating apoptosis. The ethanolic extract of G. glabra shows strong antimicrobial and cytotoxic potential and may be explored as a potential chemopreventive agent.

articles.title: Therapeutic potential of glycyrrhetinic acids: an updated patent review (2018-2024).
articles.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Glycyrrhetinic acids (GAs) are isolated from the Glycyrrhiza glabra. Interestingly, GAs and their synthetic derivatives have demonstrated numerous biological effects, including cytotoxic, antiviral, anti-inflammatory, and antimicrobial effects. AREAS COVERED: The patents granted concerning natural and synthetic GAs are covered in this review (2018-2024). The most recent patented research on GA derivatives is outlined using the search terms 'glycyrrhetinic acid' on PubMed, SciFinder, and Google Patents. EXPERT OPINION: Despite its biological effects, the further advancement and application of GA, particularly in clinical use, has been hindered by its limited druggability. This includes challenges such as low solubility and bioavailability. To enhance its biological activity and pharmaceutical efficacy, numerous research studies have focused on structural modifications, particularly to the C-3 (OH) and C-30 (CO2H) functional groups. The biological results of the C-30 amide derivatives demonstrate great potential. These modifications have produced numerous new GA derivatives with promising biological potential. The authors believe that chemists would be better off focusing their efforts on synthesizing heterocyclic analogues of GA, as this would enhance their biological activity and bioavailability. In addition, hybrid compounds of GA with other bioactive molecules could address issues of drug resistance and bioavailability.
